judgments.why: X is full of loose, dashed detail the card leaves out, such as the garden pavilion, the Turkish border, Dardanelli and David, and the remark about bankers, while Y is a short, tidy letter with a philosophical moral.
X is a lively fragment that answers the wife's doubt about leaving Paris so soon, while Y has the stock opening and closing and general feelings about home.
Y has an aside the card does not, that Kellermann was there at Stolberg's death, while X adds evening light and a made-up snuff from Bonn.
Y wanders through Milder, Torelli, the Dittmar weather forecast and Prussian professorial honour, which no model would make up from the card, while X is a neat summary.
X gives expert comparisons of the paintings (Hemling, Roger, the Correggio night against the Dresden one) and grumbles about a Würzburg fellow passenger, while Y is generic.
Y has the joke about money spent on Christians, a full cast list, the men in black and ladies in white satin, and a comparison of German and Italian singing, while X is a stock summary.
Y is a terse note with an exact arrival time of 12:07, while X adds a philosophical flourish about spirit and freedom.
Y has particulars no model would invent: owls in the moonlight, students with knapsacks, Windischmann's eye healed through prayer, and promises to show his wife the Rhine.
X gives population figures and notes on Flemish building style, while Y wraps the card in Hegelian talk about the state.
X is a broken-off fragment that misses his free Englishman among German countrymen, while Y draws a moral from facing backwards and puts the arrival in Koblenz too early.
X has details the card lacks, such as Rousseau's rose bush, plans to hear Pesaroni, and Paris two hours off, while Y draws a moral about history and spirit.
X has odd, personal turns: being glad of the rain so he could rest, and a second blossom for those who have blossomed from this land, while Y moralizes about life persisting.
Y says plainly how reluctantly he travels and how he worries about his wife's family, while X invents the Hofgarten and stars over the palace.
Y has unsure name guesses (Snell?, Creuzer?) and a dry dig at insipid colleagues, while X invents a late-night debate on logic.
X has a connoisseur's account of Lablache's voice over the chorus and the audience clapping singers off the stage, while Y is a vague summary.
X explains how the diligence's three compartments are laid out and names the play List against List, while Y is a generic letter with an invented line about wine.
X is a dated diary entry that mentions Mr. O. and green foliage despite the drought, while Y leaves Karlstein out and fills in with mood.
Y has the post leaving at 3, the godchildren, a hedge of female relatives, and a birthday in Trier, all specific and personal.
Y retells the ballet plot closely, including the joke about the Protestant 'temple', while X invents irritation and a lecture on spirit.
X is a terse passage that borrows Schiller's line about fine days in Aranjuez coming to an end, while Y pads the card with invented comforts.
X has a knowing judgment of the singers and teases his wife that he nearly fell in love with Dardanelli, while Y turns to a philosophical moral.
Y has rambling specifics such as the quarter-hour gallery, horse racing at the Champ de Mars, Lafond like a butcher, and a fond jab at his wife's liveliness.
Y answers his wife's remark that he writes with less fire than from Vienna, mentions his ill health, and has Cousin laughing at his tourist conscientiousness.
X is a plain, short description of the monument, while Y says he is still in The Hague and turns the tomb into a meditation on history.
